name: Papillary Glioneuronal Tumor

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System (2021)

criteria.description: Presence of papillary architecture with biphasic glioneuronal components on histopathological examination
Immunoreactivity for neuronal markers (e.g., synaptophysin) and glial markers (e.g., GFAP)
Well-circumscribed, cystic and solid mass on MRI typically located in cerebral hemispheres

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Histopathological confirmation of papillary architecture with biphasic glioneuronal components and positive immunohistochemical staining for neuronal and glial markers
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Molecular genetic testing may assist but is not mandatory for diagnosis.

searchTerms: seizures starting in one area then spreading
focal seizures spreading to whole body
gradual worsening of localized neurological problems
progressive weakness or numbness in one area
pain in head near tumor site
loss of part of the vision field
blind spots or missing areas in vision

common.symptomName: Nausea related to increased intracranial pressure
searchTerms: nausea caused by high brain pressure
feeling sick due to intracranial pressure
brain fluid buildup from tumor blockage
water accumulation in brain due to tumor

rare.symptomName: Endocrine dysfunction secondary to hypothalamic involvement
searchTerms: endocrine dysfunction caused by brain lesion
cranial nerve palsies causing facial or eye problems

laboratory: CSF analysis typically normal or nonspecific
imaging: MRI showing well-circumscribed cystic and solid mass with papillary architecture
T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense lesion with variable contrast enhancement
genetic: Rare reports of SLC44A1-PRKCA fusion gene
other: Histopathology demonstrating biphasic glioneuronal tumor with papillary structures
Immunohistochemistry positive for GFAP and synaptophysin

distinguishingFeatures: Predominantly astrocytic tumor without papillary architecture
Distinct molecular profile with BRAF alterations
Ependymal rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes on histology
Typically arises in ventricles or spinal cord

redFlags: New onset of focal seizures in adult
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., papilledema, vomiting)
references: Louis DN, et al. WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System, 5th Edition. IARC, 2021.
Kleinschmidt-DeMasters BK, et al. Papillary glioneuronal tumor: a distinctive neoplasm with biphasic glioneuronal differentiation. Am J Surg Pathol. 2002.
